This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Charles Snyder.
President Trump reacted to his party's midterm election losses by showcasing the new White
House ballroom.
He invited reporters to the construction project on Wednesday and only briefly addressed the
elections in which Democrats won full control of Congress.
Results are still being counted.
One of the undecided U.S. Senate races is Alaska's.
Mary Peltola is slightly ahead of Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, but as Alaska Public
Media's Liz Ruskin reports, a heavy national focus is off the state.
Alaska, it turns out, was not key to control of the Senate.
That was called for Democrats while Alaskans were still voting.
The state counts ballots until November 18.
If no candidate wins a majority, the state will tabulate ranked choices akin to an instant
runoff.
One issue dominated the last days of the race, allegations that Peltola's team helped recruit
a second candidate named Dan Sullivan.
Peltola says she was unaware.
Meanwhile, the Justice Department is appealing the dismissal of a lawsuit to withhold the
election certification if Senator Sullivan narrowly loses.
For NPR News, I'm Liz Ruskin in Anchorage.
Vice President J.D. Vance says it was the unpopular war in Iran that caused Republicans
to lose some midterm.
Here's Emily Fang reporting on Vance's social media post.
Vance has potential ambitions to run for president in 2028, though President Trump has repeatedly
declined to endorse him.
Now Vance is distancing himself further from the administration's decision to start a
war in Iran.
Writing on X, he said, "Everyone knows why we lost, and any honest conversation about
where we go from here must start there."
Vance also wrote he was "shocked" by polling data showing widespread disapproval against
his party.
High gas prices and inflation have angered American voters, many of whom blame the Trump
administration for a bad economy.
And on Tuesday night, some of those voters brought back Democratic Senator-elect Sherrod
Brown to fill Vance's vacated seat in Ohio.
Emily Fang and Pure News, the White House.
Americans weren't the only ones watching election results last night from Michigan Public Radio.
Russ McNamara has reaction from Canada.
The U.S. and Canada have been locked in a trade war that has driven up the cost of goods
on both sides of the border.
Speaking to reporters in Toronto, Ontario Premier Doug Ford says he was "doing cartwheels
down the street, seeing the returns come in."
However, he knows there is still work to be done.
"Let's do everything we can to get rid of these tariffs and show prosperity in both
countries."
The Trump administration is set to impose 50 percent tariffs on all Canadian automotive
and steel imports this January, a move that American automakers say would devastate the
industry.
For NPR News, I'm Russ McNamara in Detroit.
The New York Attorney General has appointed Jacqueline Kelly, a Cornell graduate who helped
prosecute musician Sean Diddy Combs, to be the outside counsel directing the investigation.
Kelly works for a private law firm and used to head the Criminal Civil Rights Division
in the U.S. Attorney General's office in Manhattan.
She and her team of lawyers from the AG's office and her firm will look for evidence
from the 2024 assault, including previous investigative records, and they'll also be
tasked with gathering new details and conducting fresh witness interviews.
Alyssa Nadworney, NPR News.
News contractor Lockheed Martin has agreed to pay nearly $30 million to settle claims
by the Trump administration over diversity, equity, and inclusion.
The settlement was announced Wednesday by the Justice Department and the Equal Employment
Opportunity Commission.
It resolves claims that Lockheed discriminated against white workers.
In a statement, Lockheed denied the allegations and said it agreed to the settlement to avoid
prolonged litigation.
I'm Giles Snyder, NPR News.
